doc.title: Joseph Daley interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, March 18, 2018

title: Learning to teach beginning band
summary: Starting students on mouthpieces and teaching step by step, backed by his own training.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: I wonder if you had a moment like I had, and that was when you first get in front of that band and you’re thinking okay here we go and all the kids are like looking at you or you’re trying to get them quiet. I wonder what that was like for you.

Oh yeah. Yeah, most definitely. What happens is that, as a beginning teacher, kids can sense when you’re uncomfortable. And you’ve got to be uncomfortable the first time you get in front of a bunch of kids and everything. And you have them take out their instruments and everything, you know, it can be a very trying experience. But we were trained so well. We were trained how to start a student. The first thing we did was we kind of sectioned them off, you know, your woodwinds, your brass sections and everything. And then they started with just their mouthpiece. The trumpets, and the saxophones with the reeds and everything. The drummers would have pads instead of real drums and everything. So we started them off with that, and we did exercises with them just on fundamental things, getting a sound out of the thing. Because what happens with kids is they get frustrated. If you give a student an instrument, like a full trumpet and a

mouthpiece, I mean there are buttons to press, this, the hole, then how do you get the mouthpiece in. It just becomes a frustrating thing. And then that’s how a lot of band directors get kind of screwed around and have a very disruptive program. But the approach they taught us in Manhattan was start them with the mouthpiece and everything, and then maybe a week or two later then you get the instruments out. You show them — a lot of band directors didn’t learn these techniques. You have to show the kid actually how to take the instrument out of the case and then when he takes it out of the case, where do you place the instrument. You show them where to place the instrument. Then how do you put the mouthpiece in. You don’t bang it. Then you have to tell them one turn in, one turn out, one turn in, one turn out, one turn in. And then you have them put the instrument in and you start with the mouthpiece here, just getting that buzz, and then you slowly move the buzz into the instrument and everything. So once you learn those techniques, what you do is you, the kids are learning in a system — a step-wide approach to playing the instrument, and so their frustration level is very very low at that particular point. And they progress much more rapidly. So being trained to teach students how to play instruments — and then also I grew up in music programs, all the way from elementary school. So I saw what band directors did and everything. I wasn’t just placed in front of a bunch of kids never having had that experience before in my life.
